giai_thich: They bombarded aluminum foil with alpha particles and found that aluminum continued to emit radiation even after the bombardment stopped, as some had transformed into radioactive phosphorus. This discovery allowed for the creation of radioactive isotopes used in medicine, such as for diagnosis and treatment. The Curie family has a total of 5 Nobel Prizes: Marie won two, Pierre one, and Irène and Frédéric each won one. Marie's other son-in-law, Henry Labouisse, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1965 on behalf of UNICEF.

cau_hoi: In 1999, Egyptian-American chemist Ahmed Zewail received the Nobel Prize for using ultra-fast lasers to do what?
C: Observe atoms moving during chemical reactions, on the femtosecond scale
giai_thich: One femtosecond is one quadrillionth of a second. Chemical bonds break and form in just a few tens to hundreds of femtoseconds. Zewail used laser pulses like a high-speed camera, capturing the "frames" of the reaction. This field is called femtochemistry. Zewail is the first Egyptian to win a Nobel Prize in science, and he also has a postage stamp in Egypt bearing his image.

cau_hoi: Frances Arnold won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2018, becoming the fifth woman to receive this award, thanks to what method?
A: "Directed evolution": simulating natural selection in the laboratory to create better enzymes
giai_thich: Arnold created thousands of random mutations in the gene of an enzyme, selecting the best-performing versions, and then repeating many cycles. She said: "I let nature do the hard part". The new enzymes are used to produce drugs, biofuels, replacing harmful chemical reactions. She shared the prize with George Smith and Gregory Winter. The four previous women were Marie Curie, Irène Joliot-Curie, Dorothy Hodgkin, and Ada Yonath.

cau_hoi: The 2021 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honored Benjamin List and David MacMillan for developing which new type of catalyst?
B: Non-metal organic catalyst, which are small, inexpensive, and environmentally friendly organic molecules
giai_thich: Previously, chemists mainly used two types of catalysts: metals and enzymes. In 2000, List and MacMillan independently demonstrated that small organic molecules, such as the amino acid proline, could catalyze reactions very effectively, particularly helping to produce exactly one "left-handed" or "right-handed" form of a molecule. This is crucial in drug production. List recounted that at first he thought this idea was so simple that surely someone had already tried it.

cau_hoi: Dilute solutions of potassium permanganate (purple medicine) are sometimes used for disinfection. Why does the purple color disappear when it reacts with dirt?
A: The purple color is completely dissolved by water
D: Purple-colored permanganate ions are reduced to nearly colorless or brown manganese compounds when oxidizing organic matter
giai_thich: Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer: it takes electrons from bacteria and organic matter, destroying them. At that point, manganese turns into brown manganese dioxide or nearly colorless manganese ions. Just a few crystals can dye a bucket of water purple, showing that the dispersed particles are very strong. Concentrated purple medicine can cause burns to skin and mucous membranes, so it should only be used diluted as directed. In the laboratory, it is used for titration due to its clear color change.

cau_hoi: According to "Hess's law" (1840), the energy released or absorbed in a chemical reaction depends on what?
A: It only depends on the initial and final states, regardless of how many intermediate steps the reaction goes through
B: It depends on the color of the substance
C: It depends on the reaction time
giai_thich: Swiss-Russian chemist Germain Hess discovered this law even before the law of conservation of energy was published. It's like climbing a mountain: whether you take a winding or straight path, the height difference between the base and the peak remains the same. Thanks to this, chemists can calculate the energy of difficult-to-measure reactions by adding up easier-to-measure reactions. This is the foundation of thermochemistry.

cau_hoi: How does the Arrhenius equation (1889) explain why increasing temperature makes chemical reactions occur faster?
A: Temperature creates new molecules from nothing
C: More molecules have enough energy to overcome the "activation energy barrier"
giai_thich: Molecules must collide with enough energy to react, similar to pushing a stone over the top of a hill. A rough rule of thumb: increasing the temperature by 10°C typically doubles the reaction rate. This is why refrigerators help food last longer, and pressure cookers cook faster. Catalysts work by creating a pathway with a lower "hilltop".

cau_hoi: In 1913, Leonor Michaelis and Canadian scientist Maud Menten proposed an equation describing what?
B: The reaction rate catalyzed by enzymes depends on substrate concentration and approaches a maximum value
giai_thich: When there is little substrate, enzymes are free, so the rate increases quickly with added substrate; when there is too much substrate, all enzymes are busy, and the rate reaches a maximum, like a busy checkout counter. Menten was one of the first women in Canada to earn a medical doctorate. She was also an artist, musician, spoke multiple languages, and participated in an Arctic expedition. The equation is still taught in all biochemistry courses.

cau_hoi: The Daniell cell, invented in 1836, improved the Volta cell due to which characteristic?
A: Using two separate solutions for zinc and copper, separated by a porous barrier, allowing for a more stable current over time
giai_thich: The Volta cell quickly weakens because hydrogen gas bubbles adhere to the electrodes. John Frederic Daniell placed zinc in a zinc sulfate solution and copper in a copper sulfate solution, allowing ions to pass through but not mix. The cell produces a very stable voltage of about 1.1 V and became the main power source for telegraph networks in the 19th century. The structure of the Daniell cell is still used to teach about electrochemical cells in high schools.

cau_hoi: How does the fuel cell, created by William Grove in 1839, generate electricity and where was it used?
A: Using wind; used on sailing ships
B: Combining hydrogen with oxygen to produce water and electricity; used on Apollo spacecraft
giai_thich: Unlike combustion, fuel cells allow reactions to occur on two separate electrodes, with electrons passing through an external circuit to create electricity, and the only product is water. On Apollo spacecraft, fuel cells provided electricity and produced drinking water for astronauts. In 1970, an oxygen tank supplying the fuel cell of Apollo 13 exploded, forcing the crew to use the Lunar Module as a "lifeboat." Today, there are hydrogen fuel cell cars and buses.

cau_hoi: Why is methanol (industrial alcohol) extremely dangerous if ingested by mistake, even though it looks and smells like ethanol?
C: The body converts methanol into formaldehyde and formic acid, which can cause blindness and death
giai_thich: Methanol differs from ethanol by just one carbon atom, but the liver processes it into extremely toxic substances that attack the optic nerve. As little as 10 ml can cause permanent blindness. Many poisoning cases occur due to illegally distilled alcohol made with industrial alcohol. Therefore, industrial alcohol is often mixed with bittering agents and coloring to warn users. Never drink any liquid of unknown origin, and do not store chemicals in drinking bottles.

cau_hoi: In 1897, German chemist Eduard Buchner discovered what when crushing yeast cells?
D: Cell-free extracts can still ferment sugar into alcohol, proving that fermentation is due to enzymes and does not require "life force"
giai_thich: Pasteur once believed that fermentation required living cells. Buchner crushed yeast with sand and diatomaceous earth, pressed out the liquid, and then added sugar to preserve it. He was surprised to see the liquid bubbling with CO₂: fermentation still occurred. He called the agent "zymase." This discovery opened the field of modern biochemistry, studying chemical reactions in cells. Buchner received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1907 and died in World War I in 1917.

cau_hoi: The characteristic aroma of ripe bananas primarily comes from which type of compound?
giai_thich: Esters are formed when an acid reacts with an alcohol, and many esters have fruity smells: ethyl butanoate smells like pineapple, octyl acetate smells like orange, methyl salicylate smells like menthol. Banana-flavored candies often use isoamyl acetate. Interestingly, honeybees also secrete isoamyl acetate as an alarm pheromone, so eating bananas near a beehive might not be a good idea. Food manufacturers use synthetic esters to create flavors for candies and soft drinks.

cau_hoi: How is most of the vanillin, the vanilla flavoring used in candies today, produced?
D: Synthesized from materials like guaiacol (from petroleum) or lignin (from wood), instead of being extracted from vanilla beans
giai_thich: Natural vanilla from vanilla beans is very expensive because it requires hand pollination and elaborate processing over months. In 1874, German chemists Ferdinand Tiemann and Wilhelm Haarmann first synthesized vanillin. Today, only about 1% of vanillin worldwide comes from real vanilla beans. In 2007, Japanese scientist Mayu Yamamoto even extracted vanillin from cow dung and received an Ig Nobel Prize for humor, although the method is not used in food.

cau_hoi: Why do gas companies add the smelly compound ethyl mercaptan to household gas?
B: To make the gas burn stronger
C: Natural gas is odorless, so the smell helps users detect leaks to prevent explosions
giai_thich: Methane and propane are both colorless and odorless. Mercaptan, or thiol, is a sulfur-containing compound that smells like rotten cabbage, detectable by the human nose at concentrations as low as a few parts per billion. The addition of odor became mandatory in the U.S. after a catastrophic gas explosion at a school in New London, Texas in 1937. When you smell gas, turn off the valve, open windows, do not switch electrical devices on or off, and leave the house.

cau_hoi: In 1772, Lavoisier and his colleagues conducted what astonishing experiment with diamonds?
A: Using a giant lens to focus sunlight to burn diamonds, proving it only produces CO₂ gas like coal
giai_thich: Diamonds can burn if hot enough, around 700 – 900°C in oxygen-rich air. Lavoisier placed diamonds in a sealed container and found the combustion products were identical to those when burning coal. In 1797, British chemist Smithson Tennant definitively proved that diamonds are pure carbon by measuring the amount of CO₂ produced. Thus, "eternal" diamonds, as advertised, cannot withstand a large fire.

cau_hoi: In 1991, Japanese scientist Sumio Iijima announced a new form of carbon with what shape?
A: Carbon nanotubes: carbon sheets rolled into tiny hollow tubes
giai_thich: Nanotubes have a diameter of only a few nanometers, which is about 10,000 times smaller than a human hair, yet they are very strong and conduct electricity well. They are used in lightweight composite materials for racing bicycles, tennis rackets, and are being researched for electronics and batteries. In 2006, scientists also found nanotube-like structures in ancient Damascus steel swords, which may have formed during the forging process. Some long nanotubes can be harmful to the lungs if inhaled, so they need to be handled carefully.

cau_hoi: "Tin disease" is what phenomenon that occurs with tin at low temperatures?
B: Bright shiny tin gradually turns into gray powdery tin when below about 13°C for a long time
giai_thich: This is the transformation between two allotropes of tin. The process is usually very slow but much faster at around −30°C. There are stories that tin disease damaged the buttons of Napoleon's army in Russia in 1812 or the soldered fuel boxes of Robert Scott's Antarctic expedition in 1912, but historians doubt these stories. Today, tin in solder is alloyed with other metals to prevent tin disease.

cau_hoi: Which alkali metal reacts with water so violently that it can cause an explosion immediately, stronger than sodium and potassium?
giai_thich: Alkali metals in group 1 become more reactive as you go down the periodic table because the outermost electron is further from the nucleus and easier to remove. Lithium reacts gently, sodium sizzles on the water's surface, potassium bursts into purple flames, while cesium explodes. Cesium melts at about 28°C and can melt in the palm of your hand if sealed. Cesium atomic clocks are used to define the second. Francium is below cesium, but it is highly radioactive and extremely rare.

cau_hoi: The element fluorine was first isolated by Henri Moissan in 1886 after many decades of failure. Why was this so difficult and dangerous?
C: Fluorine only exists on the Sun
D: Fluorine is the most reactive element, corrosive to almost everything, and many chemists before him were injured or poisoned
giai_thich: This period is referred to as the "martyrs of fluorine". Moissan electrolyzed liquid hydrofluoric acid at −50°C in platinum-iridium equipment and finally obtained pale yellow gas. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1906. Fluorine reacts so strongly that it ignites water, glass, and even xenon. However, compounds of fluorine like Teflon or fluoride in toothpaste are very stable and safe.

cau_hoi: Which element was the first to be artificially created in 1937 and was named after the Greek word meaning "artificial"?
giai_thich: Element 43 in the periodic table was left blank for many years, with many claiming to have found it but were wrong. Emilio Segrè and Carlo Perrier discovered technetium in a molybdenum plate bombarded in an accelerator in Berkeley (USA) sent to Italy. All isotopes of technetium are radioactive, so it is almost nonexistent in nature on Earth. Today, technetium-99m is the most widely used radioactive material in medical diagnostics, with tens of millions of uses each year.

cau_hoi: The element hafnium (number 72), named after the Latin name for Copenhagen, was discovered in 1923 thanks to whose advice?
B: Niels Bohr, who based his prediction on atomic theory that this element must resemble zirconium
giai_thich: Many chemists searched for element 72 in rare earth ores. But according to Bohr's theory, it should have properties similar to zirconium. Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy at Bohr's institute examined zirconium ore using X-rays and found it. Hafnium and zirconium are so similar that they are very difficult to separate. Hafnium absorbs neutrons well, so it is used in control rods of nuclear reactors, while zirconium is almost "transparent" to neutrons.

cau_hoi: Radon gas, a rare radioactive gas, is a health concern in some areas for what reason?
B: It has a very foul smell
D: It is generated from uranium in rocks and can accumulate in basements and airtight houses, posing a risk of lung cancer if inhaled for a long time
giai_thich: Radon is colorless, odorless, heavier than air, and tends to accumulate in low-ventilation areas. According to the World Health Organization, radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking in many countries. Radon can be measured with simple devices and reduced by ventilation and sealing cracks in floors. In 1984, Stanley Watras, a nuclear power plant engineer in the USA, continuously set off radiation alarms when he went to work, and it was discovered that the source of radiation was radon in his home.

cau_hoi: Uranium glass (vaseline glass), popular in the late 19th to early 20th century, has what notable characteristic when exposed to ultraviolet light?
giai_thich: A small amount of uranium, usually about 2%, is added to glass to create a pale yellow-green color. Under ultraviolet light, uranyl ions absorb UV light and then emit green light. This glassware has very weak radioactivity and is generally considered safe for display, but should not be used to hold acidic food for long periods. Collectors often carry small UV lights to identify uranium glass at antique markets.

cau_hoi: The Solvay process (1861) produces which important industrial chemical from table salt and limestone?
B: Soda (sodium carbonate), used to make glass, soap, paper
giai_thich: Belgian chemical engineer Ernest Solvay used ammonia as a "intermediate" that was recovered and reused, making the process cheaper and less wasteful than the old Leblanc process, which emitted hydrochloric acid gas causing severe pollution. Solvay became wealthy and funded the famous Solvay Conferences on physics and chemistry, including the 1927 conference with the legendary photo. Today, the Solvay process is still widely used around the world.

cau_hoi: Which industrial chemical is produced in the largest quantity in the world, to the extent that its production was once considered an indicator of a country's industrial strength?
giai_thich: The world produces about 250 – 270 million tons of sulfuric acid each year, primarily to make phosphate fertilizer from phosphate ore. It is also used in lead-acid batteries, oil refining, metal processing, and paper. The modern contact process burns sulfur to SO₂, then oxidizes it to SO₃ using vanadium oxide catalyst, and then absorbs it to form acid. Most of the raw sulfur is recovered from oil and gas refining processes.

cau_hoi: The Ostwald process, which helped Wilhelm Ostwald win the Nobel Prize in 1909, is used to produce which chemical from ammonia?
giai_thich: Ammonia is burned with oxygen over a platinum-rhodium grid at about 900°C, producing nitrogen oxide, which is then further oxidized and absorbed into water to form nitric acid. Nitric acid is used to produce ammonium nitrate fertilizer and many other chemicals. Combined with the Haber-Bosch process, it allows humans to convert atmospheric nitrogen into fertilizer on a massive scale. Ostwald was also one of the founders of physical chemistry and coined the term 'mole'.

cau_hoi: In a refinery, crude oil is separated into gasoline, kerosene, diesel, and asphalt by which method?
A: Fractional distillation: components with different boiling points condense at different heights in the distillation tower
giai_thich: Crude oil is a mixture of hundreds of hydrocarbons. In a distillation tower several meters high, the bottom is the hottest and the top is the coolest. Smaller molecules like gas and gasoline rise to the top; larger molecules like diesel and lubricating oil condense in the middle; asphalt is the heaviest at the bottom. Then, 'cracking' breaks larger molecules into smaller ones to produce more gasoline. Dung Quat refinery (Quang Ngai) is Vietnam's first oil refinery, operating since 2009.

cau_hoi: "Octane rating" indicated on gasoline such as RON 92, RON 95 means what?
A: The ability of gasoline to resist knocking in an engine; the higher the number, the better the gasoline can withstand compression
C: The number of kilometers traveled with 1 liter
giai_thich: The rating is compared to a mixture of isooctane (which resists knocking well, set at 100) and n-heptane (which knocks easily, set at 0). RON 95 gasoline resists knocking like a mixture containing 95% isooctane. Engines with high compression ratios require high-octane gasoline. Using high-octane gasoline does not make a car with lower octane run better. Previously, tetraethyl lead was added to increase the octane rating, but it has now been banned.

cau_hoi: The chromatography method, now used worldwide to separate and analyze mixtures, was invented by Russian botanist Mikhail Tsvet in 1903 to separate what?
C: Color pigments in leaves such as chlorophyll and carotenoids
giai_thich: Tsvet had plant extracts flow through a column of calcium carbonate powder, where the pigments adhered and moved at different rates, forming distinct color bands. He named it 'chromatography', meaning 'writing with color'. Interestingly, 'tsvet' in Russian also means 'color'. A simple experiment can be done at home: dot marker ink on filter paper and then dip the edge of the paper in water, the colors will separate. Today, chromatography is used to test for doping, analyze food, and drugs.

cau_hoi: In 1915, father and son William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg jointly received the Nobel Prize in Physics for using X-rays to do what? What record does Lawrence hold?
A: Measure temperature; he was the first person to go to space
B: Determine how atoms are arranged in crystals; he is the youngest person to win a Nobel Prize in science at just 25 years old
C: Discover new elements; he was uneducated
D: Take pictures of bones; he was the oldest
giai_thich: Bragg's law states that X-rays reflected from atomic layers in a crystal will reinforce each other at certain angles, allowing the calculation of the distance between layers. The X-ray crystallography technique later helped to determine the structures of table salt, diamonds, proteins, DNA, and hundreds of thousands of other molecules. Lawrence received the news of his award while serving in the military in France during World War I. He held the record for the youngest until Malala Yousafzai received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014.

cau_hoi: The Marsh test (1836), invented by English chemist James Marsh, helps detect which poison with very high sensitivity, marking the beginning of forensic chemistry?
giai_thich: Arsenic was a common poison because it is colorless, odorless, and easily purchased as rat poison. The test converts arsenic into arsenic gas, which when heated produces a shiny black arsenic mirror on cold porcelain, detecting amounts as low as 0.02 mg. Thanks to this method, chemists began to provide scientific evidence in court. Today, techniques like mass spectrometry are millions of times more sensitive.

cau_hoi: Why do boiled shrimp and crabs change from a grayish-blue color to orange-red?
B: Boiling water dyes the shrimp shell red
C: Shrimp absorb the color of the pot
D: Heat denatures the protein surrounding the pigment astaxanthin, 'releasing' the inherent orange-red color of the pigment
giai_thich: In live shrimp and crabs, astaxanthin is 'held' by a protein called crustacyanin, altering how it absorbs light, resulting in a blue or brown-gray shell. When cooked, the protein is denatured, releasing astaxanthin and revealing the orange-red color. The rare blue lobster has an unusually high amount of this protein. Astaxanthin is also the pigment that gives salmon its pink-orange color, derived from the algae and small crustaceans they eat.

cau_hoi: The substance luminol, described by German chemist H. O. Albrecht in 1928, is used by forensic investigators for what purpose?
A: Detecting traces of blood that have been cleaned, as it glows blue when it encounters iron in hemoglobin
giai_thich: Luminol reacts with oxidizing agents like hydrogen peroxide, and iron in blood acts as a catalyst, producing a blue light in the dark that lasts about 30 seconds. The method is sensitive enough to detect blood diluted thousands of times. However, some other substances like bleach, copper, or certain vegetables can also cause luminol to glow, so the result is only an initial screening, requiring further tests for confirmation.

cau_hoi: "Phlogiston theory" by Georg Ernst Stahl in the 18th century explains combustion how, and why was it rejected?
A: Burning materials absorb water; rejected because materials dry out
B: Fire is a living organism; rejected because fire does not eat
C: Burning materials release a substance called 'phlogiston'; rejected because metals become heavier when heated, not lighter
D: Burning materials emit sound; rejected because burning is silent
giai_thich: According to the phlogiston theory, wood loses weight when burned because it loses phlogiston, and a material stops burning in a closed container because the air has become 'saturated' with phlogiston. However, when metals are heated into 'metallic oxides', their mass increases. Some even suggested that phlogiston had 'negative mass'. Lavoisier pointed out that combustion is a combination with oxygen. Priestley, who discovered oxygen, still believed in phlogiston until the end of his life and referred to oxygen as 'dephlogisticated air'.

cau_hoi: In 1754, Scottish chemist Joseph Black discovered CO₂ and called it what?
B: "Fixed air", because it was 'fixed' in limestone and magnesium carbonate
giai_thich: Black heated magnesium carbonate and found it lost weight, releasing a gas different from ordinary air: it extinguished candles, turned lime water cloudy, and was present in breath. He was the first to demonstrate that a gas could be a distinct chemical substance. Black also discovered 'latent heat': melting ice requires heat absorption without a change in temperature. James Watt worked at Black's university, and this knowledge helped Watt improve the steam engine.

cau_hoi: In 1772, Daniel Rutherford, a student of Joseph Black, discovered which gas when he observed the "air" left after a mouse died and a candle burned out in a sealed jar that could not sustain life?
giai_thich: Rutherford removed CO₂ from the used air and found that the remaining part still killed the mouse and extinguished the candle; he called it "noxious air" or "phlogisticated air." Lavoisier later named it "azote," meaning "without life," so in French, nitrogen is still called azote, and the prefix "azo" remains in the names of many compounds. The name "nitrogen" means "niter-forming." Scheele, Cavendish, and Priestley also studied this gas around the same time.

cau_hoi: Chlorine gas was created by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in 1774. Who proved in 1810 that it was an element and named it "chlorine" after its color?
giai_thich: Scheele thought this yellow-green gas was a compound containing oxygen, and Lavoisier also believed that all acids must contain oxygen. Davy proved that oxygen could not be separated from it, so it is an element. The name comes from the Greek "chloros," meaning pale green. Scheele also discovered oxygen, manganese, barium, molybdenum, tungsten, and many organic acids, but he is rarely given full credit due to delayed publications. He had a habit of smelling and tasting chemicals, a very dangerous practice.

cau_hoi: What significant contribution did the Persian alchemist Al-Razi (9th – 10th century) make to chemistry and medicine?
B: Classifying substances into minerals, plants, and animals, describing many laboratory instruments, and distilling alcohol for medical use
giai_thich: Al-Razi was the chief physician of the Baghdad hospital, known for his careful clinical observations and was the first to clearly distinguish measles from smallpox. He described instruments such as flasks, distillation pots, funnels, and mortars. Many terms in chemistry have Arabic origins, such as "alcohol," "alkali," "alembic," and the very word "alchemy," showing the influence of medieval Islamic scholars.

cau_hoi: In 1825, Faraday discovered benzene. In 1931, Erich Hückel proposed a rule explaining why benzene is so stable. What is that rule?
A: Molecules with more oxygen are stable
B: Molecules that are blue are stable
D: Flat cyclic molecules with 4n + 2 pi electrons (like 6 in benzene) are particularly stable, called aromaticity
giai_thich: In benzene, 6 electrons do not belong exclusively to any bond but "share" around the entire ring, creating an electron cloud above and below the plane of the ring, which helps the molecule to be particularly stable. Therefore, benzene is less likely to participate in addition reactions like typical compounds with double bonds. The term "aromatic compound" originated from many compounds containing the benzene ring that were first found to have pleasant smells, such as vanillin and cinnamon, but today "aromatic" only refers to structure.

cau_hoi: Elias James Corey received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1990 for developing the "retrosynthetic analysis" method. What is the idea behind it?
D: Start from the molecule you want to create, "cut" backward into simpler pieces to find the synthetic pathway
giai_thich: Like solving a maze by starting from the exit, the chemist asks: "What pieces could this molecule be made from?" and repeats until reaching available substances. Corey used this method to synthesize hundreds of complex natural compounds, including those used as drugs. He was also a pioneer in using computers to plan syntheses since the 1960s. Today, artificial intelligence is also used to predict synthetic pathways.

cau_hoi: Female chemist Ada Yonath (Israel) received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 for determining the structure of which cellular machinery after nearly 20 years of perseverance?
A: Ribosome, the "factory" that produces proteins in cells
giai_thich: Ribosomes consist of hundreds of thousands of atoms, making it very difficult to crystallize for X-ray analysis. Yonath took ribosomes from bacteria living in the Dead Sea and hot springs because they are more stable, and used a technique to cool the crystals to very low temperatures to avoid damage from X-rays. Many colleagues once called her a "dreamer." She shared the prize with Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and Thomas Steitz. Understanding the structure of ribosomes helps design new antibiotics that target bacterial ribosomes.

chu_de: "Green chemistry" with 12 principles proposed by Paul Anastas and John Warner in 1998 aims for what goal?
B: Design products and chemical processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous substances from the start, rather than treating pollution afterward
C: Only use chemicals from green plants
giai_thich: Some principles include: preventing waste rather than treating it; maximizing the incorporation of raw material atoms into products; using safer solvents like water; using catalysts; using renewable materials; designing products that biodegrade after use. For example, the pharmaceutical company Pfizer improved the manufacturing process of a drug, reducing solvent waste from tens of thousands of liters to just a few thousand liters per ton of product.

cau_hoi: Perovskite solar cells, first reported by Tsutomu Miyasaka in 2009 with an efficiency of about 3.8%, have developed how?
C: Efficiency skyrocketed to over 25% in just about 15 years, nearly matching traditional silicon cells
giai_thich: Perovskite is the name of a type of crystal structure, named after the mineral perovskite named after Russian mineralogist Lev Perovski. Perovskite solar cells can be made by printing or coating solutions at low temperatures, cheaper than silicon. Combining perovskite with silicon into "tandem" cells has achieved efficiencies of over 33% in the lab. The major challenge is that perovskite is easily damaged by moisture, heat, and many types contain lead.

cau_hoi: In 2021, the Orca plant in Iceland began operating with what technology to combat climate change?
D: Directly sucking CO₂ from the air and then pumping it underground to react with basalt rock to form carbonate rock
giai_thich: Large fans suck air through chemical filters that capture CO₂. The CO₂ is dissolved in water and pumped deep into volcanic basalt rock, where it reacts with calcium and magnesium to form carbonate minerals in about 2 years. Orca captures about 4,000 tons of CO₂ each year, which is very small compared to the approximately 37 billion tons of CO₂ the world emits each year from fossil fuels. The costs are still very high, so reducing emissions remains a top priority.

cau_hoi: Aerogel, one of the lightest solids in the world, was first created by Samuel Kistler around 1931 after a bet. What is a characteristic of aerogel?
C: Composed of about 99.8% air, extremely good insulation
giai_thich: Kistler bet with a colleague that he could replace all the liquid in a block of gel with gas without causing the gel to shrink. He used a supercritical drying technique. Silica aerogel looks like "frozen smoke" with a light blue color. A thin piece can protect a flower placed over a Bunsen burner flame. NASA's Stardust spacecraft used aerogel to capture comet dust in 2004 without burning or breaking the dust particles.

cau_hoi: "Lotus leaf effect" causes water droplets to roll off and clean dirt from the lotus leaf. What is the reason for this?
A: The surface of the leaf has countless tiny micrometer-sized spikes covered with wax, trapping air and reducing the contact area with water.
B: The lotus leaf is electrically charged.
C: The lotus leaf is always hot.
D: The lotus leaf absorbs water very strongly.
giai_thich: German botanist Wilhelm Barthlott detailed this effect in the 1970s using electron microscopy. Water droplets almost "sit" on top of the spikes, with a contact angle greater than 150°, allowing them to roll off easily and carry dirt away. This is why lotus leaves grow from mud yet remain clean, as the saying goes, "close to mud but not smelling of mud." Scientists have mimicked this effect to create self-cleaning paints, anti-fogging glass, and water-repellent fabrics.

cau_hoi: The nickel-titanium alloy Nitinol, discovered in 1959 at the U.S. Navy laboratory, has what miraculous property?
B: Has "shape memory": it can be bent and then returns to its original shape when heated.
C: Turns into a liquid at room temperature.
giai_thich: The name Nitinol is derived from Ni (nickel), Ti (titanium), and NOL (Naval Ordnance Laboratory). According to legend, the property was discovered when a sample that had been bent multiple times was brought to a meeting, and a nearby person lighting a pipe caused it to straighten itself. The reason is that the crystal structure transitions between two phases when the temperature changes. Nitinol is used in vascular stents, orthodontic wires, and flexible eyeglass frames.

cau_hoi: In 2013, the Tan Rai aluminum plant in Lam Dong province began operations, processing which ore to produce alumina (aluminum oxide)?
giai_thich: The Central Highlands has some of the largest bauxite reserves in the world. The Bayer process dissolves aluminum oxide in the ore using hot caustic soda, separates it from impurities, and then precipitates it. Alumina is then electrolyzed using the Hall-Héroult process to obtain metallic aluminum, which is very energy-intensive. A major issue for the industry is "red mud," an alkaline waste containing a lot of iron oxide, which must be stored safely to avoid soil and water pollution.

cau_hoi: Which chemist discovered that gases combine in simple volume ratios (1808), contributing to Avogadro's hypothesis about molecules?
giai_thich: For example, 2 volumes of hydrogen combine with 1 volume of oxygen to form 2 volumes of water vapor. Dalton opposed this result because he believed that oxygen atoms could not be split in half. Avogadro resolved the contradiction in 1811 by suggesting that oxygen and hydrogen exist as diatomic molecules. However, his idea was forgotten for nearly 50 years until Stanislao Cannizzaro presented it again at the Karlsruhe Conference in 1860, the first international chemistry conference.

cau_hoi: In 2011, chemists identified "the world's bitterest compound" found in nature based on the synthetic substance denatonium. Where was it found according to the Guinness World Records at that time?
D: Denatonium is a synthetic substance; it is added to household chemicals to prevent children from swallowing them.
giai_thich: Denatonium benzoate was accidentally discovered in 1958 by the Macfarlan company in Scotland while researching anesthetics. Its bitter taste can be detected at concentrations as low as about 10 parts per billion. It is added to industrial alcohol, windshield washer fluid, antifreeze, nail-biting deterrents, and sometimes to button batteries to prevent young children from swallowing them. This is a chemical example used for safety protection.

cau_hoi: Medieval Italy and Venice were famous for Murano crystal glass. Why did the Venetian government force glassmakers to move entirely to Murano Island in 1291?
A: Because glass could only be made on the island.
B: To prevent the furnaces from causing fires in the wooden city and to keep the glass-making techniques secret.
D: Because Murano has a lot of golden sand.
giai_thich: Murano glassmakers enjoyed many privileges, their daughters were allowed to marry nobles, but they were forbidden to leave the Republic of Venice. In the 15th century, Angelo Barovier created "cristallo," a glass that is nearly as clear as crystal, by using refined plant ash to remove iron impurities. Venetian mirrors were once a luxury item throughout Europe until France lured some Murano glassmakers to make mirrors for the Palace of Versailles.

cau_hoi: Why does water have the highest density at around 4°C, rather than at 0°C?
B: Because ice is heavier than water.
C: Because water at 4°C contains more salt.
D: When cooled below 4°C, hydrogen bonds begin to arrange molecules into a loose structure similar to ice, causing water to expand.
giai_thich: This is one of the most important "anomalies" of water. In winter, the water at the bottom of deep lakes often remains around 4°C, while the colder water and ice float above, allowing fish and other organisms to survive. If water behaved like most other substances, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and could freeze solid. Water also has a very high specific heat capacity, helping the oceans regulate Earth's climate.

cau_hoi: In 1923, Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry independently proposed a new definition of acids and bases. What was it?
A: An acid is a metal, a base is a non-metal.
B: An acid is a proton donor (H⁺ ion), a base is a proton acceptor.
C: An acid tastes sour, a base tastes sweet.
D: An acid is red, a base is blue.
giai_thich: The previous Arrhenius definition only applied in water. The Brønsted-Lowry definition is broader: ammonia is a base because it accepts protons from water, even though it does not contain OH⁻ ions. Water can act as both an acid and a base depending on the substance it reacts with. In the same year, Gilbert Lewis proposed an even broader definition based on electron pairs: an acid is an electron pair acceptor, and a base is an electron pair donor.

cau_hoi: Why does human blood maintain a nearly constant pH of about 7.35 – 7.45 even when we eat acidic foods or exercise vigorously?
A: The heart filters out all the acid.
B: Blood does not react with acid.
C: Blood has a buffering system, primarily carbonic acid – bicarbonate, which neutralizes excess acid or added base.
giai_thich: A buffer solution consists of a weak acid and its salt, which can "absorb" excess H⁺ or OH⁻ ions. When blood becomes too acidic, bicarbonate ions accept H⁺ to form carbonic acid, which then breaks down into CO₂ that is exhaled; hence, when exercising vigorously, we breathe faster. The kidneys also help with long-term regulation. If blood pH drops below about 6.8 or rises above 7.8, life can be threatened.

cau_hoi: Dutch chemist Johannes van der Waals received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1910 for developing an equation describing real gases. What interesting phenomenon do van der Waals forces explain in geckos?
A: Millions of tiny hairs on their feet create weak but cumulatively large adhesive forces, allowing geckos to stick to ceilings.
C: Geckos have magnets in their feet.
giai_thich: Each gecko foot has about half a million tiny hairs, each divided into hundreds of smaller tips that are smaller than the wavelength of light. At extremely close distances, there are always temporary attractive forces between molecules due to oscillating electron clouds. In 2000, Kellar Autumn's group demonstrated that geckos adhere using van der Waals forces. Scientists have created "gecko tape" and wall-climbing robots based on this principle.

cau_hoi: "Super acid" is billions of times stronger than pure sulfuric acid and was first studied by George Olah's group. The name "magic acid" comes from which amusing event?
A: The acid glows like a ghost
C: The acid disappears when left in the dark
D: A graduate student dropped a piece of wax candle into the acid and it dissolved completely, which is something acids usually do not do
giai_thich: In 1966, at a Christmas party, graduate student Joseph Lukas dropped a piece of candle wax into a mixture of fluorosulfuric acid and antimony pentafluoride. The wax, primarily hydrocarbons that are very "inert", dissolved completely. Olah used super acid to create and observe very short-lived carbocation ions, which are important intermediates in many organic reactions, and received the Nobel Prize in 1994. Fluoroantimonic acid is even stronger than magic acid.

cau_hoi: In 2005, Yves Chauvin, Robert Grubbs, and Richard Schrock received the Nobel Prize for the "olefin metathesis" reaction. What image did the Nobel Committee use to illustrate this reaction?
B: Dancing couples swapping partners on the dance floor
giai_thich: In the reaction, metal catalysts like ruthenium or molybdenum help two molecules with carbon double bonds "swap" their halves, similar to couples changing partners. The reaction allows the creation of many new molecules with less waste, applicable in the production of drugs, plastics, and agricultural chemicals. Grubbs' catalyst is stable in air and water, easy to use, and is widely used in laboratories around the world.

cau_hoi: The 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Richard Heck, Ei-ichi Negishi, and Akira Suzuki for "cross-coupling" reactions using which metal catalyst?
giai_thich: These reactions help connect two carbon pieces accurately, using palladium as a "matchmaker" to bring two carbon atoms together. They are used to produce many types of drugs, materials for OLED screens, and pesticides. Suzuki and Negishi did not patent their method so that everyone could use it widely. The Suzuki reaction is one of the most commonly used reactions in the pharmaceutical industry.

cau_hoi: In 2001, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to William Knowles, Ryōji Noyori, and Barry Sharpless for developing a catalyst that helps produce which type of molecule?
C: Only one of the two "left" or "right" forms of an asymmetric molecule
giai_thich: Many drugs have two mirror-image forms, and our bodies, made from proteins and sugars "one-handed", react differently to each form. Knowles used asymmetric catalysts to produce L-DOPA, a treatment for Parkinson's disease. The method helps create the necessary form without wasting half of the product. This was Sharpless's first Nobel Prize; his second was in 2022 for click chemistry.

cau_hoi: Why is "decaf" coffee (caffeine-free) often made using CO₂ gas in a "supercritical" state?
B: At high pressure and temperature, CO₂ acts both as a gas and a liquid, extracting caffeine from the beans without leaving toxic solvents
giai_thich: At about 31°C and 74 times atmospheric pressure, CO₂ becomes a supercritical fluid, indistinguishable from liquid or gas. It penetrates wet coffee beans and selectively dissolves caffeine. When the pressure is reduced, CO₂ evaporates cleanly, leaving no residue. This method was developed by Kurt Zosel at the Max Planck Institute in the 1970s. The caffeine obtained is often sold to soft drink and pharmaceutical manufacturers.

cau_hoi: Why can damaged, swollen, or punctured lithium-ion batteries catch fire intensely and are very difficult to extinguish?
D: The "thermal runaway" phenomenon: exothermic reactions heat the battery, causing reactions to speed up, creating a self-amplifying spiral
giai_thich: When the separator layer between the two electrodes is damaged, internal short circuits heat the battery. The organic electrolyte solution is flammable, and the hot anode material can release oxygen, so the fire can sustain itself even in the absence of air. Therefore, do not charge batteries overnight on the bed, do not use swollen batteries, and do not use low-quality chargers. Scientists are developing safer solid-state and sodium-ion batteries.

cau_hoi: Why is liquid oxygen (light blue) attracted to the center of strong magnets, while liquid nitrogen is not?
C: O₂ molecules have two unpaired electrons, making them paramagnetic, which molecular orbital theory correctly predicts
giai_thich: According to the simple bond drawing with electron pairs, O₂ has all paired electrons and should not be attracted to magnets. Molecular orbital theory, developed by Robert Mulliken and Friedrich Hund, shows two unpaired electrons in two separate orbitals. This is a significant victory for this theory. Mulliken received the Nobel Prize in 1966. This property also explains why oxygen reacts more slowly than we think at room temperature.

cau_hoi: Why does gold have a shiny yellow color, while most other metals like silver and aluminum are silver-white?
A: Due to relativistic effects: electrons in gold atoms move very fast, altering energy levels, causing gold to absorb blue light
B: Gold has a yellow rust layer
giai_thich: Gold nuclei have 79 protons, pulling inner shell electrons to move at about half the speed of light. According to relativity, they are "heavier" and their orbits contract, narrowing the distance between outermost energy levels. As a result, gold absorbs blue light and reflects red-yellow. Without this effect, gold would appear silver-white like silver. The relativistic effect also helps explain why mercury is liquid.

cau_hoi: "Lanthanide contraction" explains what strange phenomenon in the periodic table?
A: Elements in period 6 after the lanthanide series, such as hafnium, have atomic sizes nearly equal to those of elements in the same group in period 5, such as zirconium
giai_thich: According to the rule, as you go down a group, atoms get larger. But in the lanthanide series, the electrons filling the 4f subshell "shield" the nucleus poorly, so as the number of protons increases, the atoms gradually shrink. As a result, hafnium is nearly the same size as zirconium, making the two elements so similar that they are very difficult to separate, as in the story of the discovery of hafnium in 1923. This phenomenon also makes gold and platinum very dense and "noble", with low reactivity.

cau_hoi: The Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction, discovered by Boris Belousov in 1951, has what strange feature that caused journals to refuse to publish his work?
D: The color of the solution changes back and forth periodically like a clock, which many believed contradicted thermodynamics
giai_thich: Editors thought a "oscillating" reaction could not occur, similar to thinking a pendulum could not oscillate forever. In fact, the reaction does not violate any laws, as it only oscillates when far from equilibrium and will eventually stop. Anatol Zhabotinsky, a graduate student, continued research in the 1960s. In a flat dish, the reaction creates beautiful spiral waves similar to the electrical activity of the heart. Belousov was not widely recognized during his lifetime.

cau_hoi: In 1987, Charles Pedersen, Donald Cram, and Jean-Marie Lehn received the Nobel Prize for developing "crown ethers" and supramolecular chemistry. What is a characteristic of crown ethers?
B: Cyclic molecules shaped like a crown that can snugly "embrace" a metal ion of appropriate size
giai_thich: Pedersen accidentally created crown ethers in 1967 at DuPont when an impurity in the experiment produced a strange byproduct. The size of the hole in the center determines which ion fits: small rings hold lithium, medium rings hold sodium, and larger rings hold potassium. Supramolecular chemistry studies how molecules "recognize" and bind to each other through weak forces, similar to how enzymes recognize substrates. Pedersen is one of the few Nobel laureates in science who only holds a master's degree.

cau_hoi: In 2016, Jean-Pierre Sauvage, Fraser Stoddart, and Ben Feringa received the Nobel Prize for creating "molecular machines." What notable achievement did Feringa accomplish in 2011?
A: A plane the size of a finger
C: "Nano cars" with four wheels made from a single molecule that can move across a copper surface when electrically stimulated
giai_thich: Sauvage created molecular rings that interlock like links, Stoddart created a "molecular shuttle" that moves back and forth on an axis. Feringa built a molecular motor that spins in one direction using light. The Nobel committee compared molecular machines to electric motors of the 1830s: at that time, no one knew they would lead to washing machines and electric trains. In 2017, several groups even organized the world's first "nano car race" in Toulouse, France.

cau_hoi: The 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Alan Heeger, Alan MacDiarmid, and Hideki Shirakawa for the discovery of conductive plastics. What mistake initiated this discovery?
A: A graduate student accidentally used about 1,000 times too much catalyst, creating a shiny metallic film of polyacetylene
B: Leaving the plastic out in the rain
D: Dropping the plastic into the fire
giai_thich: In 1967, in Shirakawa's laboratory in Tokyo, a graduate student misunderstood the units and added too much catalyst. The result was a shiny silver film instead of black powder. In 1977, after collaborating with Heeger and MacDiarmid, they added iodine to polyacetylene, increasing its conductivity by millions of times. Conductive polymers are now used in OLED screens, organic solar cells, and anti-static coatings.

cau_hoi: Japanese engineer Koichi Tanaka surprised everyone by receiving the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2002. Why?
C: He had never conducted an experiment
D: He only had a bachelor's degree, no doctorate, and was an ordinary company employee
giai_thich: Tanaka worked at Shimadzu Corporation. In 1985, he mistakenly mixed cobalt metal powder with glycerol instead of acetone, but still tested it and discovered that the mixture allowed large protein molecules to fly without breaking when exposed to laser light, leading to a method for protein mass spectrometry analysis. When he received the call with the news, he thought it was a joke. He shared the prize with John Fenn and Kurt Wüthrich. After the award, Tanaka became so famous in Japan that reporters followed him everywhere.

cau_hoi: German chemist Gerhard Ertl received the Nobel Prize in 2007 on his 71st birthday for research in which field?
C: Surface chemistry: reactions occurring on solid surfaces, such as on catalysts
giai_thich: Ertl used ultra-high vacuum techniques to study each step of reactions on metal surfaces. He clarified the mechanism of the Haber-Bosch process on iron surfaces and the conversion of CO in automotive catalytic converters on platinum. Surface chemistry also explains why iron rusts, why the ozone layer is destroyed on ice crystals in the Antarctic stratosphere, and how fuel cells work.

cau_hoi: Hungarian chemist George de Hevesy, a pioneer in using radioactive isotopes as "tracers," is said to have proven what about a landlady in Manchester?
A: She didn't know how to cook
B: She reused leftover food from the previous meal for the next meal, thanks to a small amount of radioactive substance he secretly added to the food plate
giai_thich: Around 1911, Hevesy suspected that the landlady was serving guests leftover food from the previous day. He sprinkled a small amount of radioactive substance into his leftover meat, and a few days later brought a detector and found that the "new" dish still emitted radiation. Although it is just a legend, it illustrates the principle of radioactive tracers, which are now used to track drugs in the body and diagnose diseases. Hevesy received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1943.

cau_hoi: American chemist Irving Langmuir (Nobel 1932) and his collaborator Katharine Blodgett invented what to reduce reflections in camera lenses and glasses?
D: Coating lenses with a thin multilayer molecular film to create "anti-reflective" lenses, nearly invisible
giai_thich: Langmuir studied thin oil films just one molecule thick on water. Blodgett, the first woman to earn a PhD in physics from Cambridge University, developed the technique to transfer each layer of film onto glass. In 1938, she created "invisible" lenses by selecting the thickness of the coating so that light reflected from both sides would cancel each other out. The technique was used for camera lenses and submarine periscope lenses during World War II.

cau_hoi: The color "Egyptian blue," created by the ancient Egyptians around 5,000 years ago, holds what significance in the history of chemistry?
A: It is a color derived from bird feathers
B: It is a color from the Nile River water
C: Considered the first synthetic pigment made by humans, created from sand, copper, limestone, and heated natron
D: It is a color extracted from lotus flowers
giai_thich: Egyptian blue is calcium copper silicate, used on statues, sarcophagi, and murals. In 2009, scientists discovered it emits strong infrared light when illuminated, helping to find invisible traces of color on ancient statues. The "Maya blue" of the Maya civilization is another achievement: a dye that tightly binds to the clay mineral palygorskite, durable enough to last for centuries in tropical rainforests.

cau_hoi: The color "Prussian blue," one of the first modern synthetic pigments, was accidentally discovered in Berlin around 1706. What important medical use does it have today?
B: As an antidote for radioactive cesium or thallium poisoning, as it retains these ions in the intestines for excretion
giai_thich: Pigment manufacturer Johann Jacob Diesbach wanted to make red but used a cochineal contaminated with animal fat, resulting in a deep blue color. Prussian blue is iron hexacyanoferrate, and although it contains cyanide groups, it is not toxic because the cyanide is tightly bound. Hokusai's painting "The Great Wave off Kanagawa" uses Prussian blue. After the radioactive contamination incident in Goiânia (Brazil) in 1987, Prussian blue was used to treat those exposed to cesium-137.

cau_hoi: In 2009, Professor Mas Subramanian's team at Oregon State University accidentally created which color, the first new inorganic blue pigment in about 200 years?
A: YInMn Blue, made from yttrium, indium, and manganese
giai_thich: The team was researching materials for electronic devices when a graduate student pulled a bright blue sample from the furnace. YInMn Blue is very stable, non-toxic, and reflects infrared rays strongly, making roofs painted with this color cooler. In 2017, Crayola released a new crayon color inspired by it called "Bluetiful." Previously, cobalt blue was discovered in 1802 and synthetic ultramarine blue in 1826.

cau_hoi: In 1880, chemist Adolf von Baeyer first synthesized indigo dye. How did this affect the world?
A: Synthetic indigo dye became cheaper and gradually replaced natural indigo, causing a significant decline in indigo farming in India.
B: Natural indigo became more expensive and more popular.
giai_thich: Baeyer spent about 17 years researching to discover the structure and synthesis of indigo. By 1897, BASF began large-scale production of synthetic indigo. Indigo is the color of today's blue jeans. In Vietnam, the H'Mong, Dao, and Tay ethnic groups still dye fabric with traditional indigo from indigo leaves, creating a distinctive deep blue color. Baeyer received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1905.

cau_hoi: What is Vantablack, announced in 2014, famous for?
C: Reflects all light like a mirror
D: Absorbs about 99.96% of incoming light, so black that three-dimensional objects look like a flat black hole.
giai_thich: Vantablack consists of billions of vertically aligned carbon nanotubes like a 'forest', allowing light to enter between the tubes and bounce back and forth until it is completely absorbed. The name is an acronym for 'Vertically Aligned Nanotube Array'. It is used in telescopes and satellites to reduce stray light. In 2016, artist Anish Kapoor purchased exclusive rights to use Vantablack in art, causing controversy and prompting other artists to create competing 'blackest' paints.

cau_hoi: According to a once-popular hypothesis, the wallpaper color 'Scheele's Green' containing arsenic may have contributed to the illness of whom in 1821?
B: Emperor Napoleon during his exile on the island of Saint Helena
giai_thich: In 1775, Scheele created a brilliant green color from arsenic copper. It was very popular in the 19th century for wallpaper, fabrics, and even toys. In damp houses, mold could convert arsenic into toxic gas. Scientists found that Napoleon's hair contained a lot of arsenic, and the wallpaper sample in his room was green and contained arsenic. However, most historians believe he primarily died of stomach illness, and the arsenic hypothesis remains unproven.

cau_hoi: What color does phenolphthalein, used as an indicator in chemical laboratories, turn in a basic solution?
giai_thich: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acid and neutral solutions, turning pink when the pH is about 8.2 or higher. It is used in titration: slowly adding a basic solution to an acid until a stable light pink color appears indicates that the neutralization reaction is complete. Phenolphthalein was synthesized by Adolf von Baeyer in 1871. For many decades, it was also used as a laxative but has been withdrawn from the market in many countries since the 1990s due to safety concerns.

cau_hoi: Why did 'fool's gold' (pyrite) once deceive many people into searching for gold?
B: Pyrite is iron sulfide with a metallic yellow color resembling gold, but it is much harder, brittle, and lighter than gold.
C: Pyrite dissolves in water like gold.
giai_thich: It can be easily distinguished: gold is soft and can be dented with teeth or a pin, while pyrite is harder and crumbles. When rubbed on unglazed porcelain, gold leaves a yellow streak, while pyrite leaves a greenish-black streak. Gold is about four times heavier than pyrite of the same volume. Interestingly, pyrite sometimes actually contains a small amount of gold hidden within its structure. When struck against steel, pyrite creates sparks, hence the name comes from the Greek word 'pyr' meaning fire.

cau_hoi: Why do chemists say 'like dissolves like', for example, cooking oil does not dissolve in water but dissolves in gasoline?
A: Polar substances dissolve well in polar substances, while non-polar substances dissolve well in non-polar substances.
B: Because the water is too cold.
D: Because oil is heavier than water.
giai_thich: Water molecules are polar, with two ends carrying slight opposite charges, attracting each other strongly through hydrogen bonds. Oil molecules are non-polar and cannot participate in that 'network', so they get pushed out. Salt and sugar dissolve in water because they are polar or ionic substances. That is why to remove oil paint stains, solvents like kerosene are needed, while water is used for water-based ink stains. Soap acts as a 'bridge' because it has both polar and non-polar parts.

cau_hoi: What does the 'Aufbau principle' in chemistry describe?
C: Electrons fill lower energy orbitals first, then move to higher energy orbitals.
giai_thich: The order of electron filling is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d..., often remembered using a diagonal diagram. Interestingly, 4s is filled before 3d because in these atoms, 4s has slightly lower energy. Some elements like chromium and copper have exceptions because half-filled or fully filled d subshells are particularly stable. The Aufbau principle, along with the Pauli principle and Hund's rule, explains the structure of the entire periodic table.

cau_hoi: In 1998, Walter Kohn received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry despite being a physicist. He was honored for developing which method?
D: Density Functional Theory (DFT), which helps calculate molecular properties from electron density instead of tracking each electron.
giai_thich: Accurately describing every electron in a large molecule requires enormous computational resources. Kohn, along with Pierre Hohenberg and Lu Jeu Sham, showed that it is sufficient to know the distribution of electron density in space. DFT has become one of the most widely used methods in computational chemistry and materials science. Kohn shared the prize with John Pople, who developed the Gaussian software. Kohn was once a Jewish child refugee who left Austria in 1939.

cau_hoi: In 2013, Martin Karplus, Michael Levitt, and Arieh Warshel received the Nobel Prize for bringing chemical experiments into where?
C: Into computers: creating multiscale models combining classical physics and quantum mechanics to simulate complex reactions
giai_thich: Simulating an entire enzyme using quantum mechanics is too heavy, but using classical physics cannot describe chemical reactions. They combined the two methods: a small part where the reaction occurs uses quantum mechanics, while the rest uses a simple classical model. The Nobel committee stated, 'Computers today are as important to chemists as test tubes.' The method is used to design drugs, catalysts, and solar cells.

cau_hoi: Rudolph Marcus received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1992 for his theory about which process, found in photosynthesis, respiration, and even in batteries?
B: The transfer of electrons between molecules
giai_thich: Marcus's theory explains why the rate of electron transfer depends on the energy required for surrounding molecules to 'rearrange'. The strangest prediction is the 'inverted region': when a reaction releases too much heat, the rate actually decreases, something many did not believe until an experiment in 1984 confirmed it. The theory helps understand how green plants convert light energy into chemical energy and how to design solar cells and organic semiconductors.

cau_hoi: In 1931, German chemist Friedrich Bergius and Carl Bosch received the Nobel Prize for developing a chemical process under what conditions?
D: High pressure, such as converting coal into liquid fuel using hydrogen
giai_thich: Bergius reacted powdered coal with hydrogen at high pressure and temperatures of about 400 – 500°C to produce fuel oil. The Fischer – Tropsch process (1925) is another method to convert coal into fuel through synthetic gas. Both were used in countries lacking oil. Today, scientists are researching using Fischer – Tropsch with CO₂ and green hydrogen to create "carbon-neutral" jet fuel. Bosch was the first to win the Nobel Prize in industrial chemical engineering.

cau_hoi: "The Transfermium Wars" from the 1960s to 1997 was a dispute over what?
A: Who discovered first and had the right to name the elements from 104 to 109, among groups in the US, the Soviet Union, and Germany
C: Who made a bigger periodic table
giai_thich: Groups in Berkeley (USA), Dubna (Soviet Union), and Darmstadt (Germany) all claimed to have created heavy elements, with different proposed names, leading to textbooks in different countries having different names. For example, element 104 was called "kurchatovi" in the Soviet Union and "rutherfordi" in the USA. In 1997, IUPAC finalized the official names: rutherfordi, dubni, seaborgi, bohri, hassi, meitneri. The name "dubni" was given after the city of Dubna as a compromise.

cau_hoi: In 2021, a scientific study confirmed what interesting fact about heavy water (D₂O) that many people had reported?
A: People taste heavy water as slightly sweet, while regular water has no taste
B: No one has tasted heavy water
D: Heavy water tastes salty like seawater
giai_thich: Heavy water and regular water are almost identical chemically, differing only in that the hydrogen atom has an extra neutron. A research group in the Czech Republic and Israel showed that the slight sweetness comes from heavy water activating sweet taste receptors on the human tongue, while mice do not like it. This indicates that even the smallest changes at the isotopic level can affect biology. Drinking a small sip of heavy water is not dangerous, but consuming large amounts over a long period can be harmful.

cau_hoi: Why is the core of a pencil called "lead" when it does not contain any lead metal?
A: Because lead is the name of a type of plant
B: When a large graphite mine was discovered in Borrowdale (England) in the 16th century, it was thought to be a form of lead because it left a gray mark on paper
C: Because pencils are made from lead but have been replaced
D: Because pencils are as heavy as lead
giai_thich: The pure Borrowdale graphite was so pure that it could be cut into sticks for immediate writing. It was called "plumbago" (like lead) or "black lead". In 1789, chemist Abraham Werner named it "graphite" from the Greek "graphein", meaning "to write". In 1795, French engineer Nicolas-Jacques Conté invented a method of mixing graphite powder with clay and firing it, allowing the creation of pencil cores with varying hardness like HB, 2B. Pencils do not cause lead poisoning.

cau_hoi: What does the Nernst equation (1889), proposed by Walther Nernst, indicate?
A: The speed of light in water
B: The number of electrons in an atom
D: The voltage of an electrochemical cell depends on the concentration of substances and temperature
giai_thich: The equation explains why batteries weaken as the reactants are consumed. It also describes the potential of the nerve cell membrane when the concentrations of potassium and sodium ions on either side of the membrane differ. Nernst also stated the third law of thermodynamics: it is impossible to reach absolute zero in a finite number of steps. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1920. Nernst also invented a type of electric lamp, selling the patent for a very high price.

cau_hoi: Gibbs free energy, proposed by Josiah Willard Gibbs in the 1870s, helps chemists predict what?
C: Whether a reaction can occur spontaneously at a given temperature and pressure, based on both energy and entropy
giai_thich: A reaction occurs spontaneously when Gibbs free energy decreases. This depends on two factors: heat released (enthalpy) and the increase in disorder (entropy). For example, ice melts above 0°C because the increase in entropy dominates, despite the process absorbing heat. Gibbs was a professor at Yale University, lived simply, and published his work in a little-read journal, so European scientists took many years to recognize his importance. Einstein called him "the greatest mind in the history of America".

cau_hoi: The VSEPR model (Gillespie – Nyholm, 1957) predicts the shape of a water molecule based on what, and what is the resulting shape?
A: Atoms attract each other; water has a circular shape
B: Atoms always line up straight; water has a linear shape
C: Atoms are arranged randomly; water has a square shape
D: Electron pairs around the central atom push each other as far apart as possible; water has a V shape, with an angle of about 104.5°
giai_thich: The oxygen atom in water has four pairs of electrons: two pairs bonded with hydrogen and two lone pairs. They arrange themselves in a nearly tetrahedral shape, but the lone pairs take up more space, narrowing the bond angle from 109.5° to 104.5°. This V shape makes water a polar molecule. If water were linear like CO₂, it would be nonpolar, lacking strong hydrogen bonds, and life as we know it might not exist.

cau_hoi: Linus Pauling introduced the concept of "hybridization of orbitals" in 1931 to explain what about the methane molecule CH₄?
B: Why methane is heavier than water
C: Why the four C – H bonds are identical and directed towards the four corners of a regular tetrahedron
giai_thich: The carbon atom has electrons in two different types of orbitals, 2s and 2p, so the bonds should not be identical. Pauling proposed that the orbitals "mix" to form four identical sp³ hybrid orbitals, with an angle of 109.5°, just as van 't Hoff predicted the tetrahedral shape in 1874. In ethylene, carbon is sp² hybridized, resulting in a flat molecule; in acetylene, it is sp hybridized, resulting in a linear molecule. The idea is a visual tool, although molecular orbital theory is more accurate in many cases.

cau_hoi: The nitrogenase enzyme in nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the roots of leguminous plants does what that humans can only achieve at very high temperatures and pressures?
A: Breaks the extremely strong triple bond in the N₂ molecule to create ammonia at room temperature
giai_thich: The triple bond between two nitrogen atoms is one of the strongest bonds in chemistry. The Haber – Bosch process requires about 400 – 500°C and pressures of 150 – 300 atm. Nitrogenase can do this at room temperature thanks to a complex metal "core" containing iron, molybdenum, and sulfur, the exact structure of which was only clarified in 2011 when it was discovered that there is a carbon atom at the center. This enzyme is very sensitive to oxygen, so the nodules in the roots contain hemoglobin-like proteins to keep oxygen levels low.

cau_hoi: The water-splitting reaction in photosynthesis, which releases all the oxygen we breathe, is catalyzed by which metal cluster in chloroplasts?
giai_thich: The atomic cluster is located in the "photosystem II" and acts like a four-step "clock": each time it absorbs a photon, it loses an electron, and after four steps, it splits two water molecules into one O₂ molecule. The detailed structure was determined in 2011 by Japanese scientists Jian-Ren Shen and Nobuo Kamiya, resembling a "skewed chair". Chemists are trying to mimic this cluster to create "artificial leaves" that produce hydrogen from water using sunlight.

cau_hoi: Why does the ocean become more acidic when the concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere increases, according to which chemical equation?
B: CO₂ + H₂O forms carbonic acid, dissociating to release H⁺ ions; simultaneously, H⁺ combines with carbonate ions, making it difficult for organisms to form shells
giai_thich: As H⁺ ions increase, they 'compete' for carbonate ions to form bicarbonate. Carbonate ions are the 'building blocks' that corals, shells, and plankton use to create calcium carbonate shells. In cold water regions like the Southern Ocean, CO₂ dissolves more, making the phenomenon more severe. Experiments show that tiny sea snail shells 'sea butterflies' are eroded after just a few weeks in water with the expected acidity by the end of the 21st century.

cau_hoi: "Raoult's Law" (1887) explains which familiar phenomenon when cooking?
A: Saltwater boils at a lower temperature
C: Saltwater boils at a slightly higher temperature than pure water because the solute lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent
giai_thich: The reduced vapor pressure means it must be heated more to reach atmospheric pressure and boil. However, with the usual amount of cooking salt, the boiling point only increases by less than 1°C, so adding salt to pasta water is mainly for flavor rather than cooking the pasta faster. François-Marie Raoult also studied the phenomenon of freezing point depression, explaining the effects of salt sprinkled on roads and antifreeze in cars. These properties depend only on the number of solute particles, known as 'colligative' properties.

cau_hoi: Most amino acids in living organisms are in the 'left-handed' (L) form, while sugars in DNA are in the 'right-handed' (D) form. How is this explained scientifically?
A: Because the Earth rotates from left to right
B: Because the Moon only shines on one side
C: Because amino acids must be very heavy
D: It remains an open question about the origin of life, with many hypotheses such as polarized light in the universe or initial random amplification
giai_thich: In the laboratory, typical synthesis reactions produce both forms in equal amounts. But life only selects one form, known as 'homochirality'. There is a hypothesis that circularly polarized light in star-forming regions creates a slight difference, which is then amplified by self-catalyzing reactions, such as the Soai reaction discovered by Japanese chemist Kenso Soai in 1995. Some meteorites carry amino acids with a slight excess of the L form.

cau_hoi: Zeolites, porous minerals with a honeycomb structure, are widely used in industry for what purpose?
A: As a catalyst for petroleum 'cracking' and to soften water in detergents due to their precisely sized pores
giai_thich: The name zeolite means 'boiling stone', given by Swedish mineralogist Axel Cronstedt in 1756 when he observed the stone steaming when heated. The pores of zeolites only allow certain molecules to pass through, so they act as 'molecular sieves'. In detergents, zeolites trap calcium and magnesium ions from hard water, replacing phosphates that cause eutrophication. In oil refining, they help break down large molecules into gasoline. Hundreds of synthetic zeolite types have been created.

cau_hoi: In the 1820s, Wöhler and Liebig discovered that silver cyanate and silver fulminate have the same formula but completely different properties. What did Berzelius name this phenomenon in 1830?
giai_thich: Silver cyanate is stable, while silver fulminate is extremely explosive despite having the same elemental composition, due to different atomic arrangements. Interestingly, Liebig and Wöhler initially suspected each other of misanalysis, then became lifelong friends. A familiar example of isomers is ethanol (drinking alcohol) and dimethyl ether (a gas) both having the formula C₂H₆O. The larger the molecule, the more isomers there are: C₂₀H₄₂ has over 366,000 isomers.

cau_hoi: In 1858, August Kekulé and Archibald Couper independently proposed which foundational idea of organic chemistry?
B: Carbon has a valency of one
D: Carbon atoms have a valency of four and can bond with each other to form long chains
giai_thich: This idea explains why there are countless organic compounds: carbon connects to form straight chains, branched chains, and rings, like Lego bricks. Couper was the first to use lines to draw bonds between atoms, the structural formula notation we still use today. Couper's paper was delayed in publication due to his advisor's hold-up, so Kekulé published first and received more credit.

cau_hoi: Alfred Werner, the first to receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for inorganic chemistry in 1913, is famous for his theory about which type of compound?
B: Complexes: a metal ion at the center bonded to many surrounding molecules or ions in a defined geometry
giai_thich: According to legend, the idea came to Werner at 2 AM in 1892, and he wrote the paper straight through until 5 PM. He proposed that metal ions like cobalt could bond with 6 groups arranged in an octahedral shape. To prove this, he isolated the mirror image forms of a carbon-free complex, disproving the notion that chirality only exists in carbon compounds. Hemoglobin in blood and chlorophyll in leaves both have metal complexes at their center.

cau_hoi: The substance EDTA, found in many foods, cosmetics, and used in medicine, works how?
A: Like a 'crab claw' tightly gripping metal ions from many sides, keeping them from reacting
giai_thich: The term 'chelate' comes from the Greek 'chele', meaning crab claw. One EDTA molecule can bind metal ions with 6 'arms' at once. In food, it holds metal ions that cause spoilage and discoloration. In medicine, chelating agents are used to detoxify heavy metals like lead. In laboratories, EDTA is used for titration and measuring water hardness. Hemoglobin and chlorophyll are also examples of metals 'held' by organic molecules.

cau_hoi: In 1965, physicist Barnett Rosenberg accidentally discovered the effect of cisplatin, one of the most important cancer treatments, how?
A: E. coli bacteria stopped dividing when an electric current passed through a platinum electrode, and the cause was the platinum compound dissolving
B: He dropped gold into a cup of water
giai_thich: Rosenberg intended to study the effect of electric fields on cell division but discovered that bacteria grew long like threads without dividing. The culprit was not the electric field but the platinum complex formed from the electrode. Cisplatin binds to DNA, preventing cancer cells from dividing. The drug was approved in 1978 and significantly increased the cure rate for certain types of cancer. Interestingly, cisplatin was first synthesized in 1845.

cau_hoi: In 1900, Moses Gomberg at the University of Michigan discovered which type of substance that was thought to be unable to exist stably?
C: The first organic free radical (triphenylmethyl), with a lone electron
giai_thich: Gomberg attempted to synthesize hexaphenyletane but obtained a yellow substance that reacted very strongly with oxygen. He realized it was the triphenylmethyl radical, with a carbon atom having only three bonds and one unpaired electron. Three large benzene rings surrounding it help stabilize it. Today, free radicals are known to play important roles in combustion, polymerization, ozone layer destruction, and even in the aging process of cells.

cau_hoi: Which type of chemical bond is considered the strongest between two atoms in a typical neutral molecule?
giai_thich: The bond in CO requires about 1,072 kJ/mol to break, stronger than the triple bond in N₂ (about 945 kJ/mol). However, CO reacts more easily than N₂ because the molecule is asymmetric and has a pair of electrons on the carbon atom that can easily be "donated." This pair of electrons allows CO to bind to iron in hemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen, making CO toxic. CO is also an important substance in the chemical industry, such as in the production of acetic acid.

cau_hoi: Which element has the highest density under normal conditions?
giai_thich: Osmium and iridium are nearly the same density, with osmium being slightly denser: a block of osmium the size of a 1-liter milk carton weighs about 22.6 kg. Lead is "only" about 11.3 g/cm³, gold about 19.3 g/cm³. Osmium was discovered by Smithson Tennant in 1803, and its name means "smell" because its oxide has a pungent odor. Osmium alloys are very hard and were once used for high-end fountain pen nibs and phonograph needles. Iridium is often found in the clay layer marking the boundary of the dinosaur extinction.

cau_hoi: Which metal has the highest melting point, around 3,422°C, and is therefore used as the filament in light bulbs?
giai_thich: Tungsten, also known as tungsten in English, means "heavy stone" in Swedish, and its symbol W comes from "wolfram." It is used in drill bits, welding electrodes, and ballpoint pen tips. Among known substances, some compounds like tantalum hafnium carbide and hafnium carbonitride are predicted and measured to melt above 3,900°C, higher than tungsten, and are being researched for protective shells for hypersonic spacecraft. Carbon does not melt at normal pressure but sublimates at about 3,600°C.

cau_hoi: Helium is the only element with which strange property related to solidification?
D: Cannot solidify at normal pressure even when cooled to near absolute zero; must be compressed at about 25 times atmospheric pressure
giai_thich: Helium atoms are very light and the attraction between them is extremely weak, while the "zero-point oscillation" due to quantum mechanics is strong enough to keep them moving, so they cannot arrange into a crystal. Liquid helium boils at about 4.2 K (−269°C), the lowest of all substances. In 1908, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes first liquefied helium. In 1926, Willem Keesom compressed helium to create solid helium for the first time.

cau_hoi: In 1954, a research team from General Electric (USA), including Tracy Hall, achieved what for the first time reliably?
C: Creating synthetic diamonds from graphite at extreme pressure and temperature
