giai_thich: Hall designed a "belt" press that achieved pressures of about 100,000 times atmospheric pressure and temperatures of about 1,600°C, along with metal catalysts. The initial synthetic diamonds were small, used for drill bits and cutting discs. Today, chemical vapor deposition (CVD) methods allow for "growing" diamonds from methane gas, producing large and clear gemstones that are chemically identical to natural diamonds. Hall was only awarded a $10 savings bond by the company.

cau_hoi: Silicone, used for baking molds, pacifiers, and sealants, differs from silicon in what way?
A: Silicone is a polymer consisting of alternating silicon-oxygen chains with organic groups attached, while silicon is an element used to make computer chips
B: Silicone is a metal, silicon is plastic
C: Silicone is made from molten sand, silicon is made from oil
D: The two words are exactly the same
giai_thich: British chemist Frederic Kipping named "silicone" in the early 20th century because he thought it resembled ketone. Silicone is heat-resistant, flexible, waterproof, and quite chemically inert, making it useful in medicine, cooking, and electronics. Pure silicon, on the other hand, is a hard gray metallic-looking semiconductor, the foundation of "Silicon Valley" in California. In English, the confusion between the words silicon and silicone is very common.

cau_hoi: In 1888, Austrian botanist Friedrich Reinitzer observed a substance extracted from carrots that had "two melting points." This discovery led to which type of material in today's phone and computer screens?
giai_thich: Cholesteryl benzoate melts at 145°C into a cloudy liquid, then becomes a clear liquid at 179°C. In between, long molecules arrange in a way similar to crystals but can still flow like a liquid. Physicist Otto Lehmann named it "liquid crystal." In LCD screens, an electric field rotates the orientation of liquid crystal molecules, controlling the light passing through each pixel. LCD screens became popular in the 1970s in pocket calculators and digital watches.

cau_hoi: In 1839, Louis Daguerre published the daguerreotype photography method based on which chemical property?
D: Silver halide compounds on a silver-plated copper plate sensitive to light, then "developed" with mercury vapor
giai_thich: The silver plate was exposed to iodine vapor to create a light-sensitive silver iodide layer. After being exposed for a few minutes, the latent image was revealed by hot mercury vapor and fixed with a salt solution. Each photograph is unique and cannot be replicated. The long exposure time meant that the first street photographs were devoid of people, as passersby could not stand still long enough. Silver halide film remained popular until digital cameras replaced it in the 2000s.

cau_hoi: In 1826, British pharmacist John Walker accidentally invented which everyday item when scraping a stick coated with chemicals on the hearth?
giai_thich: The stick coated with a mixture of potassium chlorate and antimony sulfide ignited when rubbed. Walker did not patent the invention. White phosphorus matches, which came later, were very toxic and caused severe jawbone disease in match workers. In 1844, Swedish chemist Gustaf Pasch invented safety matches: red phosphorus, which is less toxic, was placed on the striking surface of the box, while the tip of the stick contained only an oxidizer, so the stick would only ignite when struck against the box.

cau_hoi: In 1785, French chemist Claude-Louis Berthollet discovered the bleaching effect of chlorine gas. Where does the name "Javel water" come from?
A: The name of a village near Paris, where the first bleaching solution factory was located
C: The name of a river in Germany
D: The name of a type of plant
giai_thich: Previously, people bleached fabrics by sunning them in the fields for weeks and soaking them in yogurt or lye water. Chlorine could do this in just a few hours, boosting the textile industry during the Industrial Revolution. In 1789, the factory in Javel began producing potassium hypochlorite solution, later replaced by cheaper sodium hypochlorite. Berthollet was also a scientist who accompanied Napoleon on the Egyptian expedition in 1798.

cau_hoi: "The Law of Minimum" by Justus von Liebig (19th century) in agricultural chemistry is often illustrated by which image?
C: A wooden barrel with different lengths of sticks: water only fills up to the shortest stick, just as a plant only grows to the level of the nutrient that is least available
giai_thich: If the soil lacks potassium, adding a lot of nitrogen won't help the plant grow larger. The original idea was proposed by Carl Sprengel, and Liebig popularized it widely. Liebig was a pioneer in mineral fertilizers, invented the process of making beef extract, and organized one of the first modern chemistry teaching laboratories in Giessen (Germany). The Liebig condenser is still found in every laboratory, although he was not the inventor.

cau_hoi: What do Faraday's laws of electrolysis (1833 – 1834) indicate?
A: The amount of substance produced at the electrode is proportional to the total electric charge passing through the solution
C: Electrolysis does not depend on the electric current
D: All substances electrolyze the same way
giai_thich: Faraday showed that approximately 96,485 coulombs of electric charge will release one mole of a substance with a charge of 1, now known as Faraday's constant. The law suggests that electric charge exists in the smallest "parts" before the electron was discovered 60 years later. Faraday and philosopher William Whewell coined many terms still used today: electrode, anode, cathode, ion, electrolyte. The law is the basis for the electroplating industry and aluminum production.

cau_hoi: In 2000, chemists at the University of Helsinki (Finland) first created a stable compound of argon. What is it and under what conditions does it exist?
B: Argon fluorohydride (HArF), stable only at extremely low temperatures below about −246°C
giai_thich: After Bartlett created a xenon compound in 1962, krypton also had a compound, but argon is much lighter and more inert. Markku Räsänen's group irradiated a mixture of hydrogen fluoride in frozen solid argon and detected HArF using infrared spectroscopy. When warmed, it decomposes. To date, helium and neon still have no stable neutral compounds under normal conditions.

cau_hoi: In 2017, scientists announced the stable compound of helium with sodium (Na₂He) was created under what conditions?
A: At room temperature in a test tube
D: Under extremely high pressure, about over 1 million times atmospheric pressure, in a diamond anvil
giai_thich: An international team led by Artem Oganov predicted by computer and then proved experimentally by compressing sodium and helium between two diamond tips. Interestingly, helium does not actually "bond chemically" in the usual sense but helps stabilize the structure, where sodium's electrons concentrate in pairs in gaps like "ions" without nuclei. The discovery suggests that chemistry under extreme pressure may be vastly different from that on the Earth's surface, such as in the cores of giant planets.

cau_hoi: In 2017, Isaac Silvera's group (Harvard) claimed to have created "metallic hydrogen" using a diamond anvil. How did the scientific community react?
B: Great skepticism because there was only one sample, the results were not clearly reproducible, and the sample was said to have been lost during further measurements
D: The sample was displayed in a museum
giai_thich: In 1935, Eugene Wigner and Hillard Huntington predicted that under extreme pressure, hydrogen would become a conductive metal. The cores of Jupiter and Saturn likely contain liquid metallic hydrogen, generating their strong magnetic fields. Silvera reported pressures of about 495 GPa, nearly 5 million times atmospheric pressure. Many scientists believe the pressure measurement was inaccurate or that the metallic appearance was due to an aluminum oxide layer covering the anvil. The hunt for solid metallic hydrogen in the laboratory continues.

cau_hoi: In 2019, scientists confirmed that lanthanum hydride (LaH₁₀) is superconducting at about −23°C under extremely high pressure. What was the outcome of the 2023 announcement from Ranga Dias's group about room-temperature superconductivity?
A: The papers were retracted by Nature magazine due to data issues
giai_thich: Hydrogen-rich hydrides under extremely high pressure can superconduct at high temperatures because light hydrogen atoms vibrate rapidly. The Mikhail Eremets group (Germany) and Russell Hemley's group confirmed LaH₁₀ at about 250 K. However, Dias's claims about "nitrogen-doped lutetium hydride" being superconducting at room temperature were not reproducible, and an investigation concluded there were irregularities. This story, along with LK-99, serves as a lesson on the importance of independent verification.

cau_hoi: Carborane acid, synthesized by Christopher Reed's group in 2004, is considered the strongest "monoprotic" acid. What is strange about it?
A: It only exists on the Sun
C: Stronger than sulfuric acid by millions of times but less corrosive, can be stored in glass bottles
giai_thich: The acid is corrosive to glass and skin not only because it releases H⁺ strongly but also because the remaining part (anion) reacts. In carborane acid, the anion is a cage of 11 boron atoms and 1 carbon atom in a highly stable icosahedral structure, almost unreactive. Thus, it "gives" protons extremely strongly but is gentle in other respects. It can protonate even fullerene C₆₀ without breaking down C₆₀. The superacid fluoroantimonic acid is still considered stronger.

cau_hoi: In 2016, scientists in Vienna created record-long chains of "carbyne", which is what allotrope of carbon?
D: Linear chains of carbon atoms alternating single and triple bonds, predicted to be more stable than graphene
giai_thich: Carbyne is extremely reactive, so scientists could not create long chains in the air. Thomas Pichler's group "cultivated" the chains inside double-walled carbon nanotubes, achieving chains of over 6,000 carbon atoms. Calculations suggest carbyne could be the strongest material known in terms of tensile strength. In 2019, IBM even created a cyclo[18]carbon molecule consisting of 18 carbon atoms, capturing images with atomic force microscopy.

cau_hoi: In 1991, chemist Anthony Arduengo isolated a stable type of "carbene" that could be bottled. Why is this special?
B: Carbene is a molecule with carbon atoms that have only two bonds, previously thought to be too unstable to exist for long
giai_thich: Arduengo's group used large groups and nitrogen atoms alongside to protect and stabilize the "deficient" carbon atom. These "N-heterocyclic carbenes" later became important ligands in many catalysts, such as the second-generation Grubbs catalyst for olefin metathesis reactions. Interestingly, in 1960, chemist Hans-Werner Wanzlick was close to this discovery. Arduengo's carbene crystals remained stable for many years if not exposed to air.

cau_hoi: In 1981, Kenichi Fukui became the first Asian to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, sharing the prize with Roald Hoffmann. What did their work explain?
A: Why some organic reactions occur easily while others do not, based on the symmetry of molecular orbitals
giai_thich: Fukui proposed the "frontier orbital theory": reactions are primarily determined by the highest occupied molecular orbital of one reactant and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital of the other. Hoffmann and Robert Woodward proposed the "Woodward-Hoffmann rules" in 1965. Woodward passed away in 1979, so he did not receive the prize a second time. Hoffmann, who survived a genocide as a child in Poland, is also a poet and playwright.

cau_hoi: "Polywater" in the late 1960s is a famous example of what in science?
D: "Pathological science": a form of 'new' thick water that was believed to exist, but turned out to be just contaminated water
giai_thich: Soviet scientists Nikolai Fedyakin and Boris Deryagin found water condensing in tiny quartz capillaries with high viscosity, unusual boiling and freezing points. Hundreds of papers were written, and some even feared that polywater could 'infect' all water on Earth. By 1973, it was shown to be water containing impurities like silica leached from glass and sweat. Deryagin publicly admitted the mistake.

cau_hoi: In 1989, Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons claimed to have achieved "cold fusion" in which electrolysis experiment?
C: Electrolysis of heavy water with palladium electrodes at room temperature
giai_thich: They reported an unexplained excess heat not accounted for by chemical reactions and suggested that deuterium nuclei fused in the palladium crystal lattice. The news caused a global sensation due to the promise of cheap, limitless energy. However, laboratories everywhere failed to replicate the results and did not detect enough neutrons as a fusion reaction should produce. The announcement via press conference before peer review was also heavily criticized.

cau_hoi: In 2010, NASA announced a bacterium from Mono Lake (California) that was said to be able to substitute arsenic for phosphorus in DNA. What was the outcome of subsequent verification?
A: Recognized as a new form of life
C: Other groups proved the bacteria still used phosphorus; it just tolerated arsenic very well
giai_thich: Arsenic is just below phosphorus in the periodic table and has similar chemical properties, but arsenate bonds in DNA would likely be broken very quickly by water. In 2012, two papers in the journal Science showed that the GFAJ-1 bacteria needed phosphorus to grow, and its DNA did not contain significant arsenic. This event highlighted the importance of public discussion and result replication in science.

cau_hoi: In 1988, immunologist Jacques Benveniste published in Nature that water "remembers" substances that were once dissolved in it. What happened next?
B: A Nature inspection team, including a magician, supervised the repeated experiment and could not replicate the results
D: Water was proven to have memory
giai_thich: Benveniste claimed that antibody solutions diluted to the point of having no molecules still had biological effects. Nature published the article with the condition that it could be tested. The team included editor John Maddox, fraud investigator Walter Stewart, and magician James Randi. When the test tubes were secretly coded so that the experimenters did not know which was which, the effect disappeared. This is a classic lesson in "blind experiments."

cau_hoi: In 1934, German chemist Ida Noddack proposed what idea that was only recognized as correct many years later?
D: Uranium nuclei hit by neutrons can break into large fragments, i.e., fission, before Hahn and Meitner proved it about 4 years later
giai_thich: Noddack criticized Fermi's claim that he had created an element heavier than uranium, suggesting that the nucleus might have broken into lighter elements. The opinion was ignored because she did not provide supporting calculations or experiments. Earlier, in 1925, she and her husband Walter Noddack and Otto Berg discovered the element rhenium, the last stable element found in nature. She was nominated for the Nobel Prize multiple times.

cau_hoi: Which element francium (number 87), the last element discovered in nature, was found by whom in 1939?
A: Marguerite Perey, a laboratory assistant who worked with Marie Curie
giai_thich: Perey discovered francium while studying the decay of actinium. Francium is highly radioactive, with its most stable isotope having a half-life of about 22 minutes, so there may be less than about 30 g of francium in the entire Earth's crust at any given time. The name francium is derived from France. In 1962, Perey became the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences, an honor that even Marie Curie did not achieve.

cau_hoi: What does the concept of "atom economy" introduced by Barry Trost in 1991 measure in a synthesis reaction?
B: The mass ratio of the atoms of reactants present in the desired product, rather than being discarded as waste
C: The number of atoms in a mole
giai_thich: A reaction with 100% efficiency can still produce a lot of waste if most of the atoms are in byproducts. For example, addition reactions like hydrogenation can have 100% atom economy, while many substitution reactions produce unnecessary byproducts. In pharmaceuticals, there are processes that generate tens to hundreds of kg of waste for each kg of drug. This concept, along with Roger Sheldon’s "E-factor", is an important measure of green chemistry.

cau_hoi: In 2006, which book did the Royal Society of Britain vote as "the best science book ever written", with each chapter named after a chemical element?
B: "On the Origin of Species" by Darwin
C: "A Brief History of Time" by Hawking
giai_thich: Primo Levi was an Italian chemist and writer. The book, published in 1975, consists of 21 chapters, each named after an element such as argon, hydrogen, zinc, iron, gold, and concludes with a chapter on "Carbon", narrating the imagined journey of a carbon atom through limestone, air, grape leaves, and the human body. Levi writes about his work in chemistry, his youth, and memories from World War II, when his knowledge of chemistry helped him survive.

cau_hoi: "Frustrated Lewis pairs", reported by Douglas Stephan in 2006, allow for what that was previously thought only metals could do?
C: Separating hydrogen molecules (H₂) without the need for metals, paving the way for non-metal catalysts
giai_thich: Normally, a Lewis acid and a Lewis base will 'handshake' and neutralize each other. But if both have bulky groups, they cannot touch each other, like two people wanting to shake hands but wearing oversized gloves. The 'compressed' energy allows them to attack together and separate H₂ molecules. This discovery created a new field of non-precious metal hydrogenation catalysts and methods for capturing CO₂.

cau_hoi: "Single-atom catalysts", published by Zhang Tao's group (China) in 2011 with platinum atoms dispersed individually on iron oxide, have what advantage?
D: Each precious metal atom can participate in catalysis, maximizing the use of expensive metals
giai_thich: In conventional catalysts, precious metals exist as nanoparticles consisting of hundreds or thousands of atoms, but only the surface atoms are active. When metals are dispersed into individual atoms attached to a support, nearly every atom becomes useful. The challenge is to keep the atoms from 'clumping' together when heated. This field is developing rapidly, with applications in fuel cells and CO₂ conversion.

cau_hoi: To create the element tennessine (number 117) in 2010, scientists had to transport a small sample of rare berkelium from where to where?
D: From Oak Ridge National Laboratory (USA) to Dubna (Russia), in a very urgent timeframe because berkelium decays quickly
giai_thich: Only about 22 mg of berkelium-249 was produced in the reactor at Oak Ridge, which takes about 250 days. Berkelium has a half-life of about 330 days, so it had to be transported urgently. The sample was flown to Russia but was held up by customs due to paperwork, having to return to the USA once before it could go again. In Dubna, berkelium was bombarded with calcium-48 ions for about 150 days, producing 6 atoms of tennessine. The name honors the state of Tennessee, where Oak Ridge is located.

cau_hoi: In the later years of his life, Mendeleev proposed that there was an element much lighter than hydrogen in the periodic table. What did he think it was?
C: "Newtonium", a component of the hypothetical ether filling space
giai_thich: After the noble gases were discovered, Mendeleev added a "group 0" to the table and placed at the top a hypothetical super-light element, almost non-reactive, that could pass through everything, which he thought was the ether that transmitted light. He called it "newtonium", after Newton. Einstein's theory of relativity in 1905 led to the idea of ether being discarded. Mendeleev also doubted the existence of electrons and radioactivity. Even geniuses can be wrong.

cau_hoi: Before new elements were officially named, IUPAC used systematic temporary names. For example, element 118 was once called "ununoctium". What does this name mean?
A: Reading each digit in Latin – Greek roots: un (1) – un (1) – oct (8)
giai_thich: The system from 1978 used: nil (0), un (1), bi (2), tri (3), quad (4), pent (5), hex (6), sept (7), oct (8), enn (9), then added the suffix "-ium". Element 119 would be temporarily called ununennium, element 120 would be unbinilium. Temporary symbols have three letters like Uuo, Uue, Ubn. Scientists in Japan, Russia, the USA, and China are racing to create elements 119 and 120, requiring strong ion beams and many years of continuous bombardment.

cau_hoi: "Olympiadane", a molecule synthesized by Fraser Stoddart's group in 1994, has what special shape?
B: Five molecular rings interlocked like the symbol of the five Olympic rings
giai_thich: This is a "catenane" consisting of rings interlocked not by chemical bonds between the rings, but merely mechanically intertwined like links. Synthesizing such molecules requires a "template" to guide the rings to form through each other. Stoddart is humorously famous for naming the molecule. These interlocking molecules are precursors to "molecular machines" that helped him win the Nobel Prize in 2016.

cau_hoi: The CAS Registry database of the American Chemical Society, where each chemical has its own "CAS number", currently contains approximately how many substances?
B: More than 200 million organic and inorganic substances
giai_thich: Each substance is assigned a unique identifier, for example, water is 7732-18-5, helping scientists around the world refer to the same substance even if it has different names in different languages. Thousands of new substances are added daily, mostly synthesized by chemists. Although there are only 118 elements, the number of combinations can be infinite. Scientists estimate that the number of small "drug-like" molecules that could exist may reach about 10⁶⁰, more than the number of atoms in the solar system.

cau_hoi: In 2020, Andrew Cooper's group at the University of Liverpool announced a mobile "robot chemist". What did it accomplish?
D: Independently ran about 688 experiments in 8 days, autonomously deciding the next experiment, and discovered a catalyst that produces hydrogen about 6 times better
giai_thich: The robot moves around the laboratory like a person, weighs chemicals, places samples into machines, and uses intelligent search algorithms to choose the next direction, working 21.5 hours a day. Researchers estimate that a person would take several months to conduct that many experiments. Automated laboratories combining artificial intelligence are helping to find new materials for batteries, solar cells, and much faster catalysts. The robot still needs humans to ask the right questions.

cau_hoi: In 2018, scientists discovered "ice VII", a form of ice that forms under extremely high pressure, trapped inside where?
C: Inside diamonds formed deep within the Earth's mantle
giai_thich: Water has at least about 20 different forms of ice depending on pressure and temperature. Ice VII is denser than liquid water and is only stable at pressures above about 2 – 3 billion Pa. When diamonds rise to the surface, the hard diamond shell maintains pressure for the small pockets of water inside. The discovery indicates that liquid water exists about 400 – 800 km deep underground. In 2019, scientists also created "superionic ice", which is both solid and conductive, possibly existing in the cores of Uranus and Neptune.

cau_hoi: "Grotthuss mechanism", proposed by Theodor von Grotthuss in 1806, explains why H⁺ ions move unusually fast in water compared to other ions?
A: Protons "jump" from one water molecule to the next through a network of hydrogen bonds, like a line of people passing a bucket of water
B: Water pushes protons along with waves
giai_thich: Instead of a proton swimming the entire distance, it attaches to one water molecule, while another proton at the other end separates and moves to the next molecule. This is similar to a game of passing a ball in a line. Therefore, the conductivity of the acid solution is much higher than predicted. Grotthuss came up with the idea when he was only 21 years old, just 6 years after the invention of the Volta battery. This mechanism is very important in fuel cells and in the proton channels of living cells.
